final_recommendation: The room converged on a concrete path to ratification: Mexico delivers signed remediation text Wednesday evening (joint inspections, 10-day consultation window, 10%/25% tariffs on days 31/61), Congress confirms 218 votes Friday, announces January ratification vote Monday if solid, with business and labor endorsing same day. Protocol-only approach protects Canada's dairy/Chapter 19 red lines.
minority_objections: Canada insisted on ironclad guarantees that Protocol amendments would not reopen Chapter 4 (dairy) or Chapter 19 (dispute settlement)
Mexico initially resisted 30-day automatic tariffs as sovereignty violation, demanded consultation window
Some Congressional Democrats remained uncertain whether 218 votes were truly locked even after remediation text
key_conflicts: Labor union's demand for 30-day automatic tariffs vs. Mexico's sovereignty concerns and need for consultation window
Congressional demand for inspectors before ratification vote vs. Mexico's refusal to accept pre-ratification 'occupation'
Business lobby's demand for immediate certainty vs. Congress's need to verify 218 votes before announcing January vote
Tension between moving quickly (Wednesday text, Friday count, Monday announcement) vs. ensuring genuine coalition solidity
key_concessions: Labor union accepted 60-day remediation window with escalating tariffs instead of 30-day automatic tariffs
Mexico accepted joint inspections and written remediation standards in exchange for consultation window and post-ratification deployment
Congress accepted inspectors deploying post-ratification instead of pre-vote, in exchange for binding written standards
All parties accepted Protocol-only amendment approach to avoid reopening core USMCA text
red_lines: Canada: no reopening of Chapter 4 (dairy) or Chapter 19 (dispute settlement) under any circumstances
Mexico: no automatic tariffs without consultation window; inspectors only post-ratification, not pre-vote
Labor union: no endorsement without binding written remediation standards and enforceable tariff schedule
Congress: no January vote announcement without confirmed 218 solid votes, not estimates
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Whether 218 votes actually exist—Congress repeatedly deferred confirming the count, creating residual uncertainty
Risk that Wednesday remediation text reveals new gaps or triggers new demands from holdout Democrats
Mexico's domestic ratification risk—room assumed Mexico's Congress would ratify but didn't deeply probe that
Implementation risk—whether Mexico would actually cure violations within 60-day window once inspections begin
Media narrative risk if Friday count comes up short—no clear Plan B discussed
downstream_risk_variables: Actual vote count Friday—if Congress is short of 218, entire timeline collapses
Quality of Wednesday remediation text—if language is ambiguous or weak, labor/Congress may reopen demands
Mexico's domestic ratification—if Mexico's Congress balks at sovereignty implications, deal fails
Canada's legal review of Protocol carve-out language—if any ambiguity on Chapter 4/19, Canada walks
Public narrative Monday—if business/labor endorsements don't materialize simultaneously, momentum falters
uncertainty_notes: The room built a tight timeline (Wednesday text, Friday count, Monday announcement) but left critical uncertainties unresolved: (1) whether 218 votes actually exist or will emerge after remediation text; (2) whether Mexico's Congress will ratify a Protocol that includes U.S. enforcement mechanisms; (3) whether the Wednesday text will satisfy all parties or reveal new gaps. The consensus is procedural and conditional, not substantive certainty.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Dominated the room—Congress repeatedly refused to commit to January vote without confirmed 218 votes; entire discussion structured around whether deal could pass as-is or needed Protocol amendment
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver—labor union's demand for 30-day automatic tariffs opened the meeting, shaped the 60-day escalating tariff compromise, and conditioned all endorsements on binding written remediation standards
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Present and influential but not dominant—business pushed for certainty and Monday announcement, but deferred to Congress's need to confirm votes first; supported Protocol approach
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Significant but defensive—Canada's dairy red line shaped Protocol-only approach and required explicit carve-out language, but Canada mostly reacted to others' proposals rather than driving the room
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Central and driving—Mexico's refusal of 30-day automatic tariffs and demand for consultation window fundamentally shaped the 60-day compromise; sovereignty concerns structured the entire enforcement mechanism negotiation
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Present throughout but secondary—media actor repeatedly pressed for public commitments and headline clarity, but narrative concerns didn't override substantive enforcement or vote-count questions
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Dominated the room—entire discussion premised on the idea that the original USMCA package could not pass without Protocol amendment; all parties structured proposals around what amendment was minimally necessary to achieve ratification

node: Node 2 - Domestic Ratification Pressure Room (initial USMCA package formed, before the 10 Dec 2019 Protocol of Amendment; information cutoff 2019-12-09)
